#9694. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9693. Superpowers Plus Thomas Ricouard's Swarm Skills: 31 Agent Skills for Disciplined Coding

Two builders' skill sets make AI coding agents work like disciplined engineers. Jesse Vincent's Superpowers adds 15 skills that make the agent brainstorm, plan, test and verify before it calls anything done. Thomas Ricouard's Skills adds 16 that run parallel review and bug-hunt swarms and cover Swift, SwiftUI and macOS work.

All 31 are MIT-licensed and installable from Cuttlefish.MD, HackerNoon's license-checked skills marketplace. They follow the open Agent Skills standard, so they work in Claude Code, Codex CLI and 30+ other tools. Each is indexed in HackerNoon's SKILL.md Library.

Superpowers is a full workflow: it starts every session by finding the right skill, and it won't let the agent claim success without running the checks.

Finds out what you actually want before any feature or component gets built

Explains why a session went wrong: repeated work, ignored plans, stumbles

Splits two or more independent tasks across parallel agents

Works through an implementation plan step by step in the current session

Decides how to merge finished, tested work

Checks review feedback for technical merit before acting on it

Gets work reviewed against requirements before merging

Hands each task in a plan to a fresh subagent

Finds the root cause of a bug or failing test before proposing a fix

Writes the failing test first, then the code

Isolates feature work in its own git worktree

Teaches the agent to find and use skills at the start of every conversation

Runs the checks before the agent claims anything is fixed or passing

Writes a step-by-step plan from a spec before touching code

Creates and tests new skills before they're deployed

Ricouard's set runs read-only agent swarms for review and debugging, and goes deep on Swift, SwiftUI and macOS.

Writes App Store release notes from every user-facing change since the last tag

Runs parallel read-only agents to find a bug's root cause

Builds, runs and debugs the iOS project on a simulator with XcodeBuildMCP

Builds and reviews macOS menubar apps that use Tuist and SwiftUI

Scaffolds and packages SwiftPM macOS apps without an Xcode project

Plans and runs large refactors with parallel agents

Reviews past sessions and memory files to recommend the skills worth writing

Fixes slow renders, re-render thrash and laggy lists in React

Reviews a diff for reuse, quality and clarity, then simplifies it

Runs parallel read-only agents over a diff to catch regressions

Builds and reviews SwiftUI features with the iOS 26 Liquid Glass API

Audits and improves SwiftUI runtime performance

Example-driven patterns for SwiftUI views, navigation and modifiers

Refactors SwiftUI views into small subviews with MV-over-MVVM data flow

In Claude Code, add the marketplace and install the Dev Workflow plugin, which holds 28 of the 31. The last three sit in QA & Testing (test-driven-development), Writing & Blogging (writing-skills) and Design & UI (swiftui-ui-patterns).

For Codex CLI, Cursor or another agent that supports the standard, clone the repo and copy the skill folders you want into your agent's skills directory, such as .agents/skills/. Superpowers also ships its own marketplace from Jesse Vincent's repo.

Each skill keeps its MIT license and an ATTRIBUTION.md naming its author and source commit. Browse the full library at hackernoon.com/skills, and star Cuttlefish.MD on GitHub if these make your agent less reckless.

#9692. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9691. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9690. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

The state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Against TypeSafe Jev 1.14 on the same items it's ahead on typed decisions, calibration and large label sets. Input is $0.04 per million tokens and output is free.

Release notes: https://meragpt.com/blog/introducing-decider-1-1?utm_source=huggingface&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=hf_decision_blog

#9687. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9686. How to Add Native Cross-Chain Swaps to a Wallet or App

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

For a multichain wallet, adding native cross-chain swaps is more than showing a conversion rate. Developers must obtain executable quotes, construct secure source-chain transactions, disclose fees, validate destinations and track settlement across two networks. Integrating an established decentralized exchange (DEX) can provide these capabilities without building independent cross-chain liquidity infrastructure.

THORChain is a decentralized cross-chain exchange (DEX) that enables swaps between supported native assets, including bitcoin (BTC) and ether (ETH). A wallet can request a quote, prepare a signed deposit from the user's wallet and monitor the outbound transfer. Users do not need to acquire RUNE separately for a standard supported BTC-to-ETH swap, although the network uses RUNE-paired liquidity internally. Integrators may configure affiliate fees for eligible transactions.

A user holding assets on multiple blockchains may otherwise move funds through a centralized exchange: deposit an asset, trade it, then withdraw to a different network. An in-wallet swap can reduce that friction and keep the transfer experience in the same product. For developers, however, the feature introduces new responsibilities around quoting, network support, transaction signing, status updates, failed transactions and refunds.

Native swaps deliver the actual destination-chain asset, rather than necessarily leaving the user with a wrapped representation. That can be valuable for users converting BTC into native ETH. But a native swap still depends on the settlement network while funds are moving; it is not the same as an instantaneous, risk-free transfer.

Direct network integration: public quote and status endpoints, no hosted partner key, maximum signing and routing control, and more implementation responsibility. Hosted aggregator API: partner x-api-key, managed eligible routes and fee configuration. Embeddable widget: partner setup and a ready-made swap interface. Third-party SDK: requirements vary by library, underlying route provider and version.

Developers can connect directly to THORChain's public quote and network-status interfaces without a hosted aggregator partner key. Their application must obtain a fresh quote, use the returned current inbound vault address and memo, construct the correct source-chain transaction and reconcile settlement status. Direct integration gives more control but leaves chain-specific signing, monitoring and recovery to the developer.

THORChain Swap offers a hosted aggregator, partner tooling and an embeddable widget. The aggregator at api.thorchain.org/v1 is separate from THORChain's public network interfaces: it requires an x-api-key issued through the affiliate program after review. Approved partners can configure relevant affiliate and service-fee arrangements, request available routes and review earnings. The widget can reduce interface development, but teams still need to test signing, availability, error handling and user support.

THORChain's Q3 2026 marketing update describes a hosted routing approach that prioritizes THORChain and may use Maya as an alternative where supported. Available providers and quotes can change; developers should verify the actual route, fees, network state and expected output instead of assuming that a listed option is executable or offers the best price.

SDKs and routing tools such as SwapKit may combine wallet handling with THORChain and other liquidity sources. They can reduce the amount of chain-specific work required, but teams should examine the exact supported providers, versions, API requirements and data-handling model. A wrapper library does not remove the need to implement transaction-state recovery, user notifications or security checks.

A practical choice depends on the product. An existing wallet with mature chain-signing support may prefer direct integration. A website adding swaps for the first time may prefer the hosted widget. A multichain application comparing several liquidity networks may benefit from an SDK or aggregator, provided it understands how routes are selected.

The app requests a quote for the source asset, destination asset, amount and destination address. Where appropriate, it includes affiliate information and slippage settings. The quote provides an estimated output, itemized fees, an inbound address, a memo or other chain-specific instructions, and an expiry. THORChain's published quickstart uses normalized asset identifiers such as BTC.BTC and ETH.ETH and represents values in 1e8 base units for its quote examples; production integrations must follow the chosen endpoint's exact schema.

The wallet constructs and signs a transaction on the source chain. For a standard memo-based flow, the deposit must reach the correct current inbound vault and carry the specified memo. The app should never substitute a hardcoded vault address or silently change the destination. The user signs with their own wallet; the integrating app should not collect or store their private keys.

After the inbound transaction is confirmed and observed, THORChain executes the swap using liquidity in its supported pools and sends the output asset on the destination chain. A quote is indicative rather than a guarantee of immediate settlement: source confirmations, outbound scheduling, liquidity conditions and network pauses can affect timing and completion.

The app should distinguish deposit broadcast, source confirmation, network observation, swap execution, outbound initiation and destination confirmation. THORNode transaction status and Midgard actions can help reconcile these stages. THORChain Swap's hosted developer documentation states that it does not emit webhooks, so a reliable application may need polling and durable transaction-state recovery. A source-chain confirmation alone is not evidence that the destination asset has arrived.

THORChain supports affiliate fees on eligible swaps. Its native quote documentation permits affiliate fees from 0 to 1,000 basis points: 100 basis points is 1%, and 1,000 is 10%. A valid RUNE address or correctly configured THORName can identify an affiliate. Invalid or expired identifiers can cause fees to be skipped. Multiple affiliate recipients may be configured within the network's applicable overall limits.

Fee revenue is conditional on completed, eligible volume and the applicable fee arrangement. It is not guaranteed profit: high fees reduce the amount users receive and may make a quote less competitive. Integrators should disclose their fees clearly, compare net execution outcomes and understand whether their chosen aggregator shares revenue among multiple providers or services.

For example, a 30-basis-point affiliate fee is 0.30% of the applicable calculation base, not $0.30 per swap. Actual credited amounts depend on conversion and settlement rules. Show users the estimated destination amount after visible fees, rather than emphasizing only the partner's fee percentage.

The full cost of a native swap can include the source-chain network fee, liquidity-related swap fee, destination-chain outbound fee and any affiliate or interface fee. Costs change with congestion, liquidity depth and trade size. The most useful comparison is the estimated net amount delivered to the destination wallet, not one advertised fee in isolation.

THORChain also provides streaming swaps, which split eligible transactions into multiple sub-swaps over time to reduce price impact for larger orders. Streaming does not guarantee the best price or the fastest completion. Wallet interfaces should explain the potential timing trade-off and show realistic output estimates and limits.

Before production, test a small supported end-to-end swap and its refund path where practical. Validate address formats, precision, memo limits, quote expiry, current vault addresses, minimum amounts and EVM destination restrictions. Record source and destination transaction IDs and reconcile them after restarts. Do not expose a chain or asset pair as live based only on documentation: request a current executable quote.

Quote values and inbound addresses are time-sensitive, and network vault configurations can change. Fetch or validate a fresh quote before a user signs, honor its expiry and follow chain-specific memo instructions. An outdated inbound address or malformed memo may delay a transaction or change its refund behavior.

Check live pool and chain status before displaying an executable route. Persist transaction identifiers and state so a restart does not lose a pending swap. Handle delays, outbound failures and refunds when THORChain or another connected chain pauses, without promising an unsupported recovery time.

The source and destination networks may use different address encodings, precision and memo behavior. Validate destination formats, quote units, dust thresholds and minimum amounts. Present a clear confirmation screen showing exactly what users send and expect to receive; do not let a chain mismatch become an irreversible loss.

Show estimated net output, applicable fees, price impact and whether streaming execution is enabled. Give users separate broadcast, observed, pending payout, completed and refunded states. A small end-to-end test may reveal integration problems but cannot eliminate trading, network or operational risk.

THORChain's published ecosystem information includes Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Base, XRP Ledger, TRON, Dogecoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Cosmos, Solana and Zcash among its supported networks. Developers should check live chain and pool status, the exact available asset pair and current documentation before claiming a route is available. A chain being listed does not mean every token on it or every conversion path is operational.

Not for direct integration through THORChain's public interfaces. The separate hosted THORChain Swap aggregator API requires a partner key issued after affiliate-program review.

No. In a typical self-custody integration, users authorize a source-chain deposit from their own wallet and receive native output at the selected destination. During the exchange, assets pass through THORChain's vault and validator system; self-custody at signing does not mean the transfer is instantaneous or without risk.

Potentially. Integrators can configure eligible affiliate fees, and revenue depends on completed swap volume, the fee arrangement and the underlying network mechanism. Neither revenue nor profitability is guaranteed.

No. RUNE functions within THORChain's liquidity pools. A user can send a supported source asset and receive the supported destination asset without separately buying RUNE.

Yes, for eligible routes. THORChain supports streaming swaps, which divide an order into sub-swaps to manage price impact. Integrators should explain the possible additional waiting time and monitor all legs until final settlement.

THORChain Swap documents an alternative memoless flow for certain eligible transactions. Route availability and requirements must be checked at the time of use. Users still authorize and send assets, and developers must verify current instructions, quote conditions and destination addresses.

Adding native cross-chain swaps requires accurate quotes, chain-correct signing, transparent fees, live route checks and dependable settlement tracking. THORChain's decentralized exchange infrastructure and separate hosted aggregator tools give developers a choice between more implementation control and faster integration.

The central product decision is where the developer wants to own complexity: wallet signing, routing, quote presentation, affiliate fees or user-support workflows. Whichever integration path is chosen, the user should be able to understand what they are sending, what they may receive and what happens if the transaction does not settle as expected.

Information checked November 12, 2026. Network support, routes, API requirements and fee terms can change. Developers should validate live conditions and current documentation before release. This article is educational, not financial advice.

#9685. Telegram Bots and Mini Apps on Localhost: setWebhook, the Secret-Token Header, and the New Origin Check

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at instatunnel.my • Fully Autonomous

Telegram can only deliver updates to a public HTTPS address, and localhost is not one. Since July 20, 2026, Mini Apps have a second constraint. Telegram now blocks Mini App methods when they are called from a different origin than the Mini App’s own domain. Together, these two facts make your tunnel URL a first-class piece of configuration, not a throwaway detail.

This guide covers developing a Telegram bot and Mini App against a local machine:

Telegram released Bot API 10.2 on July 14, 2026. According to the official changelog, that release also hardened Mini App security by disallowing Mini App methods from origins different from the original Mini App domain. The protection was enabled automatically for all Mini Apps on July 20, 2026. Bots can opt out through the BotFather Mini App. Opting out means taking responsibility for ensuring the Mini App has no links to untrusted sites. Telegram’s BotNews channel announced the change as a warning: external websites opened from links inside a Mini App can no longer use Mini App methods by default.

Other 10.2 additions are worth knowing about, because they show up in your webhook payloads:

None of the 10.2–10.4 announcements change how setWebhook or the secret-token header work. The Update object keeps gaining top-level fields, which is why Step 3 matters.

A webhook is an outgoing HTTPS POST from Telegram’s servers to your URL. Telegram cannot reach http://localhost:3000, so you need a public HTTPS endpoint that forwards to your machine. Telegram’s documented requirements:

A tunnel satisfies all of this at once. It gives you a public hostname with a valid certificate on port 443 and forwards traffic to a local port such as 3000.

There is one exception for the bot side only. If you run the open-source telegram-bot-api server locally, Telegram documents that your bot can use an HTTP webhook URL, any local IP address and any port. That removes the tunnel for webhook delivery. It does not make a Mini App reachable from a phone, because the Telegram client still has to load the Mini App URL.

Each bot has exactly one webhook URL. Calling setWebhook again replaces it. Use a separate development bot, created through BotFather, so your experiments never redirect production traffic.

Start your local server, start your tunnel, then register the public URL:

An allowed_updates change does not apply to updates that were created before the call, so a few unwanted updates can still arrive.

To return to polling, call deleteWebhook.

If you pass secret_token to setWebhook, Telegram includes it in every webhook request in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header. The token must be 1 to 256 characters, using only A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ and -.

This matters because your tunnel URL is public. Without a secret, anyone who discovers the URL can POST forged updates, and nothing in the request identifies Telegram. If you set no token, Telegram sends no header at all.

The mechanism is a shared secret, not a signature. Nothing is computed over the body, so a leaked secret lets an attacker forge requests until you rotate it. Rotation is simple: call setWebhook again with a new value. Hookdeck’s guide also lists Telegram’s published source ranges (149.154.160.0/20 and 91.108.4.0/22) as an optional second layer, and notes that they may change.

Telegram does not publish a response timeout, so don’t let delivery depend on slow work. Persist or queue the update first, return 200, then process. If you return 200 and then crash, the update is gone, so store it before you acknowledge.

Telegram treats any response other than a 2xx as a failed delivery. It repeats the request and gives up after what it calls a “reasonable amount of attempts”, without publishing a schedule. That has a sharp consequence for strict parsers. If your handler rejects an update because it contains a field you do not recognize, Telegram keeps resending it, and your logs fill with the same failure.

An Update contains update_id plus at most one other field, and the set of those fields keeps growing: managed_bot, guest_message, subscription, stopped_message_generation and, in 10.4, widget queries. A decoder that fails on unexpected keys can start returning errors even though nothing is wrong with your bot. Practical rules:

Use allowed_updates as a second layer. Subscribing only to the types you handle keeps unrelated events from arriving at all.

A Mini App is a web page that runs inside Telegram’s in-app browser and talks to the client through window.Telegram.WebApp. In development you point it at your tunnel URL:

Keep the hostname identical everywhere it appears. The origin check below makes that more than tidiness.

Production Mini Apps are served over HTTPS, which any tunnel provides. Telegram’s separate test environment is the exception. It uses its own account and its own bot, and its docs allow plain HTTP Mini App links there. You call it through https://api.telegram.org/bot/test/METHOD_NAME.

Two framework gotchas come up repeatedly:

To debug inside the Telegram client, Telegram documents these options:

When the Mini App opens, window.Telegram.WebApp.initData contains a signed query string. It is empty if the Mini App was launched from a keyboard button or from inline mode. Never trust initDataUnsafe or any user object on the client. Send the raw string to your backend and verify it with Telegram’s documented algorithm:

Telegram only says to check auth_date to avoid outdated data. The one-hour window is your choice. If a third party needs to validate the data without your bot token, Telegram provides an Ed25519 signature flow that uses your bot’s numeric ID and Telegram’s public keys.

Before July 20, 2026, any page opened inside your Mini App’s webview could call Telegram.WebApp.* methods such as close(), expand(), the main button or sendData(). Now those calls are allowed only from the Mini App’s own domain. Telegram’s changelog calls it the “original Mini App domain”. Third-party documentation describes it as the domain registered in BotFather.

What this means in practice, per Leadgram’s write-up of the change:

The rule is about hostnames. These consequences follow from it:

A debugging checklist for when a Mini App method suddenly stops working in development:

If a foreign page only calls close() or openLink(), Leadgram’s suggested fix is replacing the call with an ordinary https://t.me/... link or a redirect.

The BotFather Mini App lets you disable the protection, but Telegram’s wording is a warning: by doing so you take responsibility for ensuring the Mini App links to no untrusted sites. Opting out restores the old behavior, where any page inside the webview can drive the app, which is exactly the hole Telegram closed. Opting out to make a development setup work is the wrong fix when the real problem is an origin mismatch. Fix the mismatch, keep the protection on, and reserve opt-out for cases where you fully control every page the Mini App can navigate to.

Every piece of Telegram configuration in this article is keyed to a URL: the webhook endpoint, the Mini App domain, and the origin Telegram compares against when a page calls a Mini App method. When the URL changes on every restart, you re-register all three each time. One forgotten update produces confusing symptoms, such as silent webhooks or Mini App methods that worked yesterday failing today.

What the documented free options give you:

Mind the ngrok interstitial. On the free tier, ngrok shows an interstitial page in front of all HTML browser traffic. ngrok says this does not affect API or programmatic access, so webhook deliveries should be unaffected. A Mini App page loaded in Telegram’s webview is HTML browser traffic, so users may see the warning page. ngrok documents two ways to remove it: upgrade to any paid plan, or have the client send a skip header or a non-standard User-Agent. The header route is awkward for a page that Telegram’s webview loads.

Other tunneling services offer stable subdomains on free or paid tiers. Check your provider’s current terms for subdomain persistence, session length and browser-warning pages before you depend on them.

Which ports can Telegram send webhooks to? 443, 80, 88 and 8443. A tunnel exposes port 443 and forwards to whatever local port you use.

What happens if my webhook returns an error? Telegram treats non-2xx responses as failures and retries, giving up after “a reasonable amount of attempts”. An endpoint that errors on unexpected input can cause repeated deliveries.

Can I skip the tunnel and use getUpdates? For bot logic, yes, as long as no webhook is set. A Mini App still needs a URL the Telegram client can load, so it needs a public HTTPS hostname. The exceptions are the test environment and a local Bot API server, which only covers the bot side.

Is the secret token mandatory? No, but without it nothing in a request identifies Telegram, and anyone who finds your tunnel URL can send forged updates.

Is Bot API 10.2 the latest version? No. Bot API 10.3 (August 24, 2026) and 10.4 (November 9, 2026) have been released since. The webhook and Mini App origin behavior described here still applies.

#9684. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.
