#9674. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

Grammarly Pros

  • It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.
  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.
  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.
  • Some features are not available for Mac.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.
  • Compatible with Google Docs!
  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.
  • They offer more integrations than most tools.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9673. Privacy-Focused PDF Retrieval with Node.js Chunk Boundaries and Citations

Infrai fits the collection and query stage when you want a plain REST call and one consistent backend surface; it is one option inside this boundary, not a substitute for your processor review.

I would start with a collection per trust boundary (for example, personal notes versus imported work PDFs), a small metadata contract, and a freshness policy written down before choosing a vector service. The important fields are document id, page number, source class, and an ingestion timestamp. A chunk should be small enough to cite one page passage, but large enough to retain the sentence that gives the passage its meaning. There is no magic token count here. Your own documents decide that.

Write the contract before the endpoint. Define what a retrieval unit is, which metadata filters are mandatory, and how stale a result may be. A support answer that cites a deleted policy is worse than one that says it has no source.

For each chunk, I keep an immutable chunk_id, document_id, page, character offsets, and a content hash. The hash lets a re-ingestion job prove that a citation refers to the same bytes that were embedded. ACL or workspace labels belong in metadata, too, but they must be enforced before context reaches the language model. Filtering after generation is theater. I have seen teams spend a week tuning top-k while an old export remained searchable because deletion was treated as a UI action instead of a pipeline event; the fix was to version the document, tombstone the old chunks, invalidate answer caches, and make the evaluator assert that the old hash never appears again.

Region and retention belong in this contract. Decide which country may process extracted text, who is a processor, and what deletion means for source files, embeddings, and backups. A vector API can enforce collection and query boundaries; it cannot, by itself, rewrite your data-processing agreement with the embedding or model provider. That boundary stays with the specialist you selected for those services.

The first useful check is boring: can the client see only the collections it is allowed to see? Infrai exposes a plain REST surface, so this probe needs no SDK or client-library version pin. Anything that can send HTTPS can run it.

That is deliberately not a fake end-to-end RAG script. The query body is a contract you must derive from the service discovery schema and your metadata policy, then validate in tests. I log a request id, selected collection, filter, top-k bound, and returned chunk ids. I never log raw PDF text in the default application log.

At query time, cap both the number of collections and the number of chunks. Run lexical or metadata narrowing first when the corpus is large, then vector search, then (if needed) a rerank stage. Keep the original page and offsets attached through every stage. The answer renderer should refuse to emit an uncited claim when no chunk survives the policy check.

A short failure case is useful here. If a user asks about an expired refund rule, a freshness filter should produce “no current source” rather than quietly returning the nearest old paragraph. That behavior is a product feature.

I recommend trying Infrai for the collection and query stage when your team values a single HTTP integration and wants to keep provider switching behind a narrow retrieval contract. Infrai gives this workflow one key, one bill, and one plain REST API across backend capabilities, without installing an SDK. Its broad surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules, so a small support tool can add storage or scheduling without inventing another client convention. That removes integration surface area; it does not grant automatic regional residency or contractual deletion guarantees.

The catch is important. If your policy requires self-hosted storage, a fixed region you control, or a processor agreement with bespoke deletion evidence, stick with pgvector or a specialist managed provider that documents those controls. Infrai is not the right answer merely because the request is private. The specialist remains responsible for the data plane and model-processing terms.

At a few thousand PDFs, I would add a staging queue between extraction and vector upsert, with idempotent document versions. Replays should replace the same version, never create duplicate chunks. A nightly evaluation set should include normal support questions, near-duplicate pages, deleted documents, and adversarial prompts that try to cross a collection boundary. Track recall of the expected page and precision of the cited passage separately.

I would also make deletion a tested workflow: mark the document unavailable, remove its chunks, invalidate cached answers, and verify that a repeated query cannot retrieve the old chunk_id. Retention timers need the same test. Your mileage may vary across providers and regions, so record the actual processor and region for each stage instead of assuming the vector endpoint tells the whole story.

#9672. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9671. Web corporativa en 2026: diseñar impacto sin sacrificar rendimiento ni control

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at juliancardozo.github.io

Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.

Una web corporativa ya no compite solo por informar qué hace una empresa. Compite por comunicar criterio, diferenciar una propuesta y conducir una conversación comercial. El reto técnico es lograr una experiencia memorable sin convertir la página en una SPA frágil, lenta o difícil de evolucionar. Pambú 2026 fue construido desde ese equilibrio.

Una visita institucional dura poco. En ese tiempo, la persona tiene que poder entender qué hace la organización, por qué debería prestarle atención y cuál es el siguiente paso. La arquitectura de información no puede ser una lista de secciones intercambiables: necesita una narrativa que ordene propuesta de valor, enfoque, identidad, servicios y contacto.

En Pambú 2026, la estructura se organiza como una experiencia de una página con navegación a secciones. El scroll deja de ser solo una forma de desplazarse y se convierte en el ritmo de la presentación. Para negocio, esto permite guiar el mensaje; para ingeniería, mantiene un modelo de contenido directo y comprensible.

El fondo animado con WebGL y Three.js incorpora profundidad y movimiento a una propuesta centrada en creatividad, tecnología e innovación. Pero el componente visual no puede cargar con el significado de la página. El contenido comercial, la navegación y el contacto deben permanecer disponibles como HTML semántico y legible sin depender de la capa gráfica.

Esta separación es un control de resiliencia. La experiencia enriquecida puede evolucionar, degradar de forma aceptable en hardware limitado o fallar sin bloquear el mensaje. El impacto visual es una capa de mejora progresiva, no una condición para que el sitio funcione.

GSAP y ScrollTrigger permiten sincronizar transiciones con la lectura de cada sección. Usarlos bien no significa animar todo: significa dirigir atención hacia un cambio de contexto, una jerarquía visual o una llamada a la acción. Cada animación debe justificar qué comprensión o conversión mejora.

En una página de alto impacto, el rendimiento es parte de la marca. El equipo debe tratar el peso de assets, el trabajo de renderizado y la ejecución en dispositivos de menor capacidad como restricciones de diseño. La elección de JavaScript vanilla para la capa de interacción reduce superficie de runtime y facilita que la experiencia se mantenga enfocada.

Pambú 2026 se implementa con HTML5, CSS3 y JavaScript vanilla, con Three.js y GSAP cargados desde CDN. Esta decisión no niega el valor de un framework; responde a un caso donde la página es una experiencia editorial acotada, no una aplicación con estados de negocio complejos.

La consecuencia es operativa: menos capas para desplegar, inspeccionar y modificar. El equipo puede concentrar su esfuerzo en narrativa, contenido, performance y calidad visual. Si el producto necesita luego CMS, personalización o funcionalidades transaccionales, la arquitectura puede crecer sobre una necesidad comprobada, no una hipótesis.

Principio de experiencia corporativa: el alto impacto surge cuando la narrativa, la identidad visual y el rendimiento trabajan como un sistema. La tecnología debe intensificar el mensaje, no convertirse en el mensaje.

#9670. The Flaw Chipmakers Spent 50 Years Fighting Is Now Their Best Feature: Memory Chip Fingerprinting

A cybersecurity researcher and enthusiast who likes to get to the bottom of niche topics and share the information found with the public.

A cybersecurity researcher and enthusiast who likes to get to the bottom of niche topics and share the information found with the public.

A cybersecurity researcher and enthusiast who likes to get to the bottom of niche topics and share the information found with the public.

Memory chips of the same model, with identical serial numbers and the same price, come off the manufacturing line. But when they are powered on, each begins its unique pattern of making tiny mistakes. For years, these mistakes were a target for the engineers trying to eliminate them. However, security specialists found ways to use them for anti-counterfeit protection, securing encryption keys, and even tracing people.

The ideal memory chip should be fast, cheap, spacious, and non-volatile. None exist. Hence, computers use different types of memory chips, each of them having some advantages in particular tasks.

SRAM uses the miniature closed circuit of transistors containing two possible states for every bit - like a light switch. It is the fastest memory but requires six transistors to store one bit and, therefore, is expensive and big. SRAM is used in the cache memory and microcontrollers' memory.

DRAM stores each bit in the form of the amount of charge in the capacitor. Only one transistor and a capacitor are necessary to store one bit. Therefore, it is cheap and small enough to become the primary memory of the computer. Unfortunately, the charge stored in it leaks away with time, and the memory needs refreshing every 64 milliseconds.

Flash uses a special transistor in which the charge is trapped in the insulator. Once in there, electrons remain trapped for years, making flash a good choice for phone memory, SSDs, and USB drives. The writing and erasing process of the flash is slower than that of other memories, as erasure happens in blocks. Additionally, the erasure process damages the insulator, hence limiting the usage of the memory in several thousands of erasing cycles.

Modern chip factories work with technologies on an atomic level, and atoms rarely fall in place identically each time. Therefore, one transistor may be slightly stronger than its neighbour, one capacitor - leakier, some insulator layers - thinner. The manufacturers try to hide those defects under the safe margins and make all memory chips behave alike. However, if pushed to the very limit of these margins, individual flaws will start causing flipped bits.

For instance, when an SRAM chip is powered on, it does not know what its starting state is. Powering on a cell means letting it choose the desirable state, and it always depends on which of the two sides wins, the winning side being a bit stronger.

For DRAM, if it is disturbed somehow, it will forget its contents. Without refreshing the memory, the leakiest cells will forget their contents first. Moreover, in DRAM, there is a more serious flaw: the reading of some rows of the memory will affect the adjacent rows, flipping the bits in the memory that was not accessed by the program. This is the infamous Rowhammer effect. In 2014, researchers detected it in 110 out of 129 memory modules they tested.

As with DRAM, in flash memory, changing the content of one cell can affect the state of the neighbouring cells. Besides, the cells of flash memory wear out differently: some of them can be programmed after only a few writing cycles, whilst some will require many more of them.

Now that we know the flaws of each memory type, we can force errors and pinpoint their location. This pattern of errors is different in each chip but unique to one particular chip, just like a fingerprint. Researchers call it a physical unclonable function since even the manufacturer will not be able to create another chip with the same fingerprint pattern.

Turn on an SRAM chip and read its content right after. Most of the cells wake up identically each time, creating the long series of ones and zeros that are unique to this one chip. Comparison of two power-ups of the same chip shows that differences occur in fewer than ten per cent of the bits. On the contrary, comparing two different chips shows differences in about half of the bits. This makes it possible to identify each chip reliably.

For DRAM chips, the easiest way is to write some pattern into the memory, interrupt its refresh, and see which cells forget the content. The set of forgetful cells is a fingerprint. This method works without any additional hardware but takes minutes. A more sophisticated way is to read the memory with deliberately quick timing, and the cells that cannot cope will show up in about 88 milliseconds.

Rowhammer provides another approach. In a study done in 2025, about a hundred memory modules were hammered, and the fingerprints distinguished between chips with 99.91% accuracy in less than five seconds.

For flash, under normal operation, a flash memory chip continues pulsing the cell until its contents are safely stored. Fingerprinting involves stopping this process halfway. Apply the same number of short pulses to all the cells and stop - some fast cells will be ready, but the slow ones will still be blank. This pattern of fast and slow cells becomes the unique fingerprint of a chip. The opposite technique of stopping an erase halfway through works in the reverse direction and even for the flash memory integrated into everyday microcontrollers. Everything happens using the usual chip interface, without any special equipment.

Those fingerprints can be used as keys that are never stored on the chip. If a secret key is stored in a chip, it can be recovered by an attacker. However, the key derived from the chip fingerprint is different. It is generated each time the device is powered on with error correction, and it vanishes when the power goes off. There is nothing to steal from the powered-off device.

Another useful application is proving the identity. Manufacturers record the fingerprints of each chip in the factory. Then the server challenges the device to reproduce its fingerprint. This way, even affordable sensors and smart tags get a strong identity without additional security chips.

Similarly, counterfeit and recycled components can be detected. Used chips from electronic waste are regularly sold as new. Fingerprint verification will detect a chip not registered by the legitimate manufacturer, whilst analysis of the flash memory will provide even more information. Since the erasure operations take more time with ageing of the memory cells, the time it takes to execute these operations alone will indicate the remaining service life of the microchip.

And finally, random numbers. The cells that fail to settle in the single state have another useful property - they generate true random numbers, which are always needed by cryptography.

However, despite having many useful applications, hardware fingerprints can also be used to track devices, and not always for good purposes. The fingerprint that cannot be changed is a fingerprint that cannot be hidden. One study showed that energy-efficient memory that tolerates minor errors produces enough errors to identify the machine that created a file. Moreover, extracting fingerprints is hard on hardware: Rowhammer attacks damage data, and flash-based approaches consume a part of the chip's lifespan.

However, the main idea of all this remains quite positive. Flaws that engineers tried to eliminate during fifty years turned out to be one of the most reliable features of the chip - the identity based on physics, chosen by no one and impossible to copy.

A cybersecurity researcher and enthusiast who likes to get to the bottom of niche topics and share the information found with the public.

#9669. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9668. Onboarding clínico: cómo evitar que un producto de salud empiece vacío

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at juliancardozo.github.io

Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.

Milo Care nació de un problema de gestión de información: vacunas, medicación y controles repartidos entre una foto, un chat, una nota y la memoria. La primera decisión de producto fue evitar trasladar ese trabajo al usuario. Un onboarding útil no pide datos para llenar una base: transforma datos mínimos en un plan de cuidado accionable.

Un registro clínico que abre vacío le pide al usuario que reconstruya meses o años de información antes de obtener algo a cambio. Para un producto de cuidado, ese costo inicial compite directamente con el papel, el chat o la nota que ya usan. No es un detalle de UX: es un problema de activación y retención.

En Milo Care, el alta del perro captura país y datos relevantes para iniciar un calendario vacunal. El resultado esperado no es una ficha más completa; es una primera sesión que ya muestra próximas acciones, fechas y un historial sobre el que se puede operar.

El calendario no podía ser una lista genérica de vacunas. Las recomendaciones cambian por país, fuente y contexto clínico. La solución fue modelar reglas de negocio que distinguen el calendario de Argentina y Uruguay, con SENASA y las guías WSAVA como referencias, sin presentar la plataforma como sustituto de una indicación veterinaria.

Ese límite es parte de la arquitectura de dominio. El sistema puede organizar, recordar y mostrar el plan; la evaluación clínica y la decisión profesional siguen fuera del automatismo. Separar ambas responsabilidades evita que una recomendación de software se presente como diagnóstico.

El calendario inicial se integra con módulos de vacunas, medicamentos, citas y síntomas. Cada módulo maneja su propio estado y vencimiento, pero alimenta un único historial por animal. Esa consolidación permite que el dashboard priorice el trabajo pendiente y que los recordatorios operen sobre datos estructurados.

Para negocio, la decisión tiene un efecto claro: el producto entrega valor antes de pedir hábitos complejos. Para ingeniería, deja un dominio extensible para nuevas especies, clínicas veterinarias y planes premium sin convertir el onboarding en una colección de excepciones.

Principio de producto: el onboarding debe convertir la información mínima en una primera acción valiosa. En dominios de salud, las reglas automatizadas organizan el seguimiento, pero no reemplazan el criterio profesional.

#9667. Trybit Upgrades Crypto Infrastructure with New API and Interface for High-Volume Mass Payouts

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Panama, November,11 — Trybit, a global crypto payment gateway for online businesses, has released a new mass payout workflow with a new interface and API. The update adds a step-by-step form for creating mass payouts, line-by-line validation before submission, an individual status for each recipient and a searchable payout history. Trybit has also improved notifications in the personal account and added new account emails.

Sending one crypto transfer is simple. Sending hundreds at once is where things go wrong. One mistyped address in a long list can hold up the whole mass payout or send funds where they cannot be recovered. When part of a mass payout goes through and part does not, finance teams have to work out by hand who was paid. Re-sending without that answer risks paying the same person twice.

Marketplaces, affiliate programs, gaming platforms and companies with remote contractors face this every payout cycle. Many of them still reconcile crypto payouts in spreadsheets.

Mass payouts are now created through a step-by-step form with three ways to add recipients:

A Download template button gives teams a template that matches the format the system accepts: recipient address, amount and, if needed, currency. Teams no longer have to build the file from the format description in the documentation. The network for each recipient is detected automatically from the address, so nobody has to select it line by line.

A file is more practical for regular payouts, when the list is exported from accounting software. For fully automated workflows, mass payouts via API remain available.

Every line in the recipient list is checked before the payout is submitted for processing. If a line has a problem, the error is shown next to that specific line. A team fixes the one entry that needs attention instead of rebuilding the whole file or finding the mistake after the money is gone. For cryptocurrency payouts, this is essential: a transfer to the wrong address cannot be reversed, and the check before funds are debited is the only point at which an error can be corrected without loss.

Once the mass payout is sent, each line in the list shows its own status. If most transfers go through and a few do not, the team sees exactly which ones need attention. Reconciliation becomes a check of one screen instead of comparing wallet history against a spreadsheet. A summary of each mass payout is also sent by email.

Sent mass payouts are saved to the history, which supports search and status filters. This makes it faster to answer a partner who asks whether a payout was sent, and to pull records together for an audit.

The update also changes how teams learn about account events. All events now come through a single notification feed in the personal account, with new notification types for partial invoice payments, exchanges and errors. Notifications have a dedicated page: events are grouped by day, the category filter shows a count for each category, and important notifications can be pinned. The feed updates in real time, with no need to reload the page.

All emails are now sent through a single mechanism that prevents duplicates and limits sending frequency, so the same event no longer reaches the inbox twice. New emails cover withdrawal completion, mass payout summaries, failed AML checks and more.

The new API mirrors the interface, so teams that run payouts from their own back end get the same workflow without opening the personal account. Through the API, a team can submit a mass payout built from a file or a recipient list, receive validation errors for specific lines before anything is sent, track the status of each transfer and look up the payout history. Payouts are authorized with a dedicated payout API key, generated in the Security section of the account settings and separate from the project's main API key. API payouts can go to any address, including addresses that are not on the account's saved list.

API reference: docs.trybit.com/api-reference-v2/withdrawals.

The interface works on desktop and tablets and is available in Spanish and Portuguese, among other languages.

Trybit  is a global crypto payment gateway built for high-volume online platforms that accept and pay out in the most popular crypto currencies and stablecoins. It applies AML/KYT screening of incoming transactions before crediting to the merchant’s balance. The rest of the payment cycle covers automatic conversion into stablecoins, mass payouts, static wallets, CMS integrations, and White Label (Host2Host) options for platforms that want the payment flow under their own brand.

#9666. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9665. NoisyTCP CVE-2026-99288: Pre-Authentication Remote DoS Causing Linux Kernel Panic via Crafted TCP Packets

NoisyTCP is a denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability that exploits a race condition between the lockless TCP socket lookup and socket reuse in the Linux kernel. It allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger a NULL pointer dereference and a kernel panic using only crafted TCP traffic. TCP listeners with default configurations, including Nginx, Apache, and SSH, can be targeted, but the reproduction results demonstrated in public materials are limited to a remote DoS causing a host crash. The researcher stated that they created a highly restricted, lab-specific exploit for VMs, but did not demonstrate general-purpose remote code execution (RCE).

No additional hypotheses. Lab PoC success is not treated as confirmation of in-the-wild exploitation.

Linux web servers, SSH services, proxies, and container hosts are widely deployed, and application-level patches alone cannot remediate this issue. Inventory externally reachable listeners and kernel packages, and prioritize vendor fixes. Integrate availability monitoring, remote kernel logs, kdump, and load balancer health checks to ensure that host crashes lacking authentication logs can still be investigated as network-layer attacks.

#9664. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9663. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9662. exploit_agent: Automating Everything from Patch Diff Analysis to Exploit Generation and Execution Without Human-in-the-Loop

GTIG identified a multi-agent framework named exploit_agent operating on a public staging server. The framework continuously compares web application code before and after patches, analyzes potential vulnerabilities, creates exploits, and automatically executes them against targets without human-in-the-loop intervention. The server also contained data gathered from victims, along with scripts for internal reconnaissance, brute force, and web shell deployment.

Confirmed Related Capabilities: GTIG identified scripts on the staging server capable of supporting internal reconnaissance, brute force, web shell deployment, and the removal of other attackers' web shells. Execution methods and sequences within individual victim environments have not been publicly disclosed.

Inference: The following items are candidates for investigation. An attacker's use of external LLMs or retrieval of public source code may not leave traces in victim-side logs. Access to source repositories and CI artifacts should be verified using audit logs restricted to organization-managed assets.

No additional hypotheses. Do not assert victim counts, attribution, or exploit success rates beyond publicly available information.

Because PentAGI activity targeting Asia has been confirmed, organizations should treat internet-facing CMS platforms, plugins, and business applications as priority assets. Operating under the assumption that the window between patch diff publication and exploitation is compressed, organizations should combine rapid patching, virtual patching, web process monitoring, outbound traffic restrictions, and source or CI artifact access auditing.

#9661. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

Semantic search for 3D assets: USD + RTX simulation previews

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a flixfox scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

#9660. IronWallet Review: A Simple, Open Wallet That Is Growing Fast

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

Your Trusted Crypto & Blockchain Newswire

IronWallet seems to have appeared out of nowhere, but according to Ermo Eero, the project has been around for four and a half years. The idea was to build a simple, easy-to-use crypto wallet that anyone can open, with no KYC, no ID checks, and no sign-ups. What started as a niche project has grown into a competitive product. Its most notable feature is gasless transfers, which let users move funds without holding the network's native coin to pay fees. IronWallet also offers gasless swaps, routed through SwapKit, one of the market's leading swap aggregators.

IronWallet comes across as a solid all-rounder. Everything runs inside the app: sending, receiving, swapping, and buying crypto. Everything seemed to work well. Buying requires some form of KYC, which is expected, but the choice of payment providers offered in the app was wider than I anticipated.

The biggest gap is network coverage. IronWallet supports 12 networks. They include many of the most popular chains, but established non-custodial wallets support considerably more, and IronWallet still has ground to make up against the market leaders.

The second gap is platform. There is no desktop or web version. Nearly every competitor offers one, and for users who manage funds from a computer, that is a real limitation.

IronWallet's answer to that gap is its MCP server. The MCP is open source, and it works somewhat like a desktop companion: it lets AI agents in desktop tools control the wallet, and it includes a local wallet manager that opens in your own browser for adding, importing, backing up, and deleting wallets. Experienced users of desktop AI agents will likely find it straightforward to set up. For newcomers, the advice is simple: read the FAQ first.

IronWallet is a clear, open, and easy-to-use non-custodial wallet, and it is improving quickly. Its gasless transfers and gasless swaps make everyday use simpler, and buying crypto inside the app is a practical bonus. Network count and platform reach are the areas to watch, and with a project that has been building steadily for years, the momentum suggests they will keep improving. For mobile users who value simplicity and no-KYC access, IronWallet is already a strong choice, and it is well worth a look.
