#9558. Green Bean Casserole

Green bean casserole belongs on every Thanksgiving spread. If you're scrambling to figure out how to perfect the classic side dish, look no further. I ditched the cream of mushroom soup for a homemade cream sauce and fresh sautéed mushrooms, but don’t worry—this dish is still super-simple to make. You only need 8 ingredients and a little over an hour to make it. Keep reading on for my top tips to make this classic side dish the best it can be:

What People Are Saying:"Once you have this, you'll never be able to go back to the Campbell's gray sodium laden sludge & soggy canned green beans recipe! This is amazing! Your whole family will change their minds about green bean casserole." - CyanCarrot

"This is the best green bean casserole I've ever made! It was easy enough that I could read it through twice, and then just make the dish without having to refer to the text of the recipe! It turned out great, my family ate it up! Without using a can of condensed soup, I could control the amount of salt...this made from scratch sauce tastes more mushroomy than a can of condensed soup!" - GreenBike

The very first step is blanching the green beans. This may seem a little fussy, but it's the best way to start cooking the beans to preserve their crispy texture and bright green color as they continue to bake in the oven. It's easy, but just requires a little setup. Cook the beans in salted water for a few minutes, then immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking process. That's it!

On to the aromatics! This is what takes this casserole truly over the top. Cook sliced onions in butter until just starting to soften, anywhere from 7 to 10 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and let everyone get to know each other. Make it even better by adding some garlic; in my opinion, the more, the merrier. Your kitchen will smell amazing. Pour the aromatics into the bowl with the blanched beans.

Time for the sauce. No need to wipe out the pot, just melt a stick of butter, then toast the flour.

Slowly pour in the milk and whisk, letting the sauce come to a simmer, until nicely thickened. Be sure to taste for salt and pepper.

Add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

Time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

Some tips: Make sure to let it cool to room temperature before baking, or add a couple of minutes to your timer to adjust to the colder temperature. Whatever you do, DON'T forget to add the fried onions until after the first round of baking. If they're added before refrigerating, they'll get soggy instead of having that signature crispy crunch.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container (or cover your casserole dish with storage wrap) before refrigerating. This side will last up to 4 days refrigerated (look through our Thanksgiving leftovers ideas for some creative inspo for what to do with them), and leftovers can be reheated in the microwave or oven.

#9556. The Chain Italian Sub With The Best Bread, According To Customer Reviews

Italian sub sandwiches are a thing of beauty: cured meats piled high, creamy cheese, a bit of lettuce and tomato, perhaps a slather of mayo if you're feeling controversial, and maybe a drizzle of herb-infused oil and vinegar. You can find them at pretty much any sandwich shop or deli, though naturally, a number of factors, like size and overall quality, will vary. And while the meats and cheese might be the stars of the show, you cannot discount the importance of good bread. According to a Food Republic roundup of the 10 best chain Italian subs, New York-based chain DiBella's stood out on account of just that, with customers particularly praising its signature everything bread, which adds an extra layer of savory flavor thanks to its topping of seasonings, including ingredients like garlic, poppy seeds, and sesame seeds.

For example, one Reddit user shared that DiBella's version of an Italian, called the Godfather, did not disappoint. "The 'everything' bread was the best part [in my opinion]," they wrote, "but the whole sub was pretty [top-tier] as far as chain restaurants go."

Another reviewer on Yelp also specifically cited the Godfather, saying it was extremely flavorful. "[It] was ridiculously good. So much flavor and taste. The bread really sealed the deal," they praised.

If the glowing reviews have you hankering for a sandwich from a chain you've never heard of before, you're not alone. The reason DiBella's mostly flies under the radar is that it is actually quite limited in locations. As of November 2026, the chain is only present in five states, with the majority of its locations concentrated in New York, its home state, and Ohio. And for the first 80 years of its existence (DiBella's was founded in 1918 as a grocery store), it consisted of just one Rochester location. That changed in 1998, when the company opened its second location, and since then, DiBella's has seen a flurry of expansion, with 2024 proving especially busy.

However, the smaller chain size might actually contribute to the quality of the bread that has put DiBella's on the map, since fewer locations make it easier to maintain standards. For now, in all 44 of the sandwich shop's restaurants, the bread gets baked at least twice daily, as the final step in a process that takes more than half a day. Before the rolls go in the oven, though, the dough gets aged for a minimum of 16 hours to improve texture and taste. Then, seasonings are manually sprinkled on top, and finally, someone wielding a knife hand-scores the tops of the loaves. The frequency of this baking process means that you will almost assuredly get sub rolls at their peak freshness whenever you place your order at DiBella's.

#9554. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9553. Olive Garden's Buttery Breadstick Topping Is Actually Dairy-Free

Many diners would agree that one of the biggest pleasures of dining out at Olive Garden isn't just the ambiance or even the appetizers or entrees, like the Tour of Italy, but rather one of the complimentary items that comes with your meal: breadsticks. These soft, pillowy sticks of dough are buttery, garlicky, and great for dipping into dressing or sauces. They are so popular that the chain of Italian-inspired restaurants goes through a staggering number each week, and many diners may even request some extra when taking home leftovers. But despite the buttery flavor of this signature item, it doesn't actually contain any real butter. Instead, the company uses margarine.

Margarine differs from butter in that it is made from oils with a variety of additional ingredients, including water. Together, they form an emulsion that can resemble butter. While not all brands of margarine are completely dairy-free, the kind Olive Garden uses doesn't contain any dairy at all, making it suitable for diners with dairy allergies or those who abstain from animal-derived foods. One reason Olive Garden may use margarine instead of butter is that it can provide a smoother, more consistent topping for its breadsticks.

Butter can also resolidify after it cools, potentially giving the breadsticks a pasty coating. According to Reddit users, Olive Garden uses liquid margarine, which retains its consistency. Additionally, margarine is generally less expensive than butter, and in an industry with razor-thin margins, anywhere you can save money can lead to greater profits.

Perhaps the best use of margarine for Olive Garden fans is to recreate a homemade version of its iconic breadsticks. You can start by using Great Value Garlic Bread Sticks — a fantastic store-bought dupe, available at Walmart — and brushing melted margarine over the sticks after they're heated for an extra buttery finish. Or you can use the melted margarine to give new life to any of the chain's leftover breadsticks you bring home.

Margarine's uses extend well beyond breadsticks, though. For starters, many types of margarine retain a soft texture even when refrigerated, meaning you can easily spread it onto bread or toast even when it's cold. Try doing that with regular butter! Because some types of margarine contain little to no milk solids, they also don't burn as easily as traditional butter does. This means that you can use them to pan-fry foods at relatively higher temperatures than you can with butter without as much risk of altering the flavor of the finished dish.

Finally, margarine is also great for baking. You can often use it in place of butter in the same quantities, though the substitution may affect the finished product. Certain types of margarine also remain solid at higher temperatures, which can be beneficial when baking things like pastries, where fat that melts too quickly can make the difference between beautiful, puffy layers and a flat, greasy end result. Just be sure to avoid spreads or squeezable margarine for baking, as the water content can be too high and negatively affect your recipe.

#9551. I Tried Taco Bell’s New FLAMIN’ HOT Menu Items To See If They Really Bring The Heat

One of these could've used a few extra sauce packets.

I'll try just about anything Taco Bell puts on its menu, and whatever I order usually ends up drenched in hot sauce. So when I heard the chain was adding a new FLAMIN' HOT offering (and bringing back a punchy fan favorite), I was curious whether they'd finally give me enough spice to leave those packets alone. I like my food hot enough to get a few beads of sweat forming on my nose, and with a name like FLAMIN' HOT, I don't think that's asking too much.

There were two contenders: the returning FLAMIN' HOT Grilled Cheese Burrito ($5.49), which I'd missed during its first run, and the brand-new FLAMIN' HOT Mini Taco Salad ($2.49). Both feature Fritos FLAMIN' HOT, so I figured I was in for some decent spice. Here's how that worked out.

I love a good taco salad, especially when the bowl itself is edible. But my first impression of this mini version was that it looked like a pretty ordinary Taco Bell salad. And after a few bites, I wasn't finding much to convince me otherwise.

You've got seasoned beef, refried beans, lettuce, tomatoes, cheddar, and Creamy Chipotle sauce tucked into a crispy flour tortilla bowl. Beneath everything was a layer of reddish rice, which Taco Bell says is seasoned with FLAMIN' HOT Fritos. I could definitely see the color, but whatever was making that rice spicy wasn't doing much for my taste buds.

And speaking of Fritos, I'm still trying to figure out where mine went. They're supposed to be in there, but I genuinely couldn't tell whether they'd been included in my particular serving. I would've loved more of the chipotle sauce, too, because the other ingredients seemed to overpower whatever heat was hiding underneath.

The shell itself was fine, although a little bland and greasy. I’m still pro-taco salads, but I just wish the spice had been more noticeable—especially with a name that makes such a big promise.

The returning burrito is stuffed with seasoned beef, spicy rice, crunchy FLAMIN' HOT Fritos, nacho cheese sauce, sour cream, and Creamy Chipotle sauce. And because Taco Bell clearly believes there's no such thing as too much cheese, the entire thing gets a three-cheese blend grilled onto the outside of the tortilla.

I took a pretty substantial first bite, making sure to get into those Fritos and all its FLAMIN’ HOT components. The nacho cheese had that gloriously gooey, movie-theater quality (complimentary), while the rest of the fillings worked together much better than they had in the salad. There's a lot happening inside this thing, and I was enjoying every bit of it.

Most importantly, I could actually taste the heat. There was a satisfying punch of spice, followed by that little tickle at the back of my throat that tells me something's doing its job. I wasn't desperately reaching for a drink, but the burrito had enough kick to make me happy.

I even went back for another bite of the mini taco salad afterward, and it tasted better with the burrito's lingering heat still in my mouth. Who knew it needed a little help from its menu companion?

Ultimately, the burrito is the one I'd order again. The mini taco salad has potential, and for $2.49, I wouldn't be opposed to giving it another shot. But next time, I'm bringing the extra hot sauce packets it should've saved me from needing.

#9549. Not Bacon: Give Grilled Cheese A Southern Twist With This Hearty Ingredient

Giving your grilled cheese a Southern twist doesn't mean you have to start using buttermilk biscuits and lard. Instead, you can use ham hocks, a seasoning meat that isn't always actually eaten but is always enjoyable.

The same thing that makes ham hocks delicious also makes them a bit difficult to use. Loaded with bone, connective tissue, and extremely tough meat, bringing out their flavor potential requires a lot of low-and-slow cooking. You may have more luck using smoked ham hocks for a deeper cure and smoke profile, though both smoked and raw hocks still require a long simmer to fully break down the tough collagen before transferring the meat to a sandwich. Regardless, adding shredded ham hock to grilled cheese gives you a tender, protein- and fat-laden ingredient that practically melts right alongside your gooey cheese.

Ham hocks are especially good when you "reuse" them. Cooking one dish with ham hocks and then using the meat in another lets you easily transfer complex flavors, a major tip for making any grilled cheese better. Hocks cooked in Southern-style collard greens adopt a perfectly moist texture and pick up acidity from vinegar and vegetable notes from the greens and onions. Similarly, ones cooked with black-eyed peas have a next-level creaminess, adopting earthy aromas to round out your sandwich. Still, if you want to preserve the smokiness of a fresh smoked ham hock, you can always simmer it for a couple of hours until the meat and skin fall apart, giving you a budget-friendly alternative to pulled pork.

Using ham hocks in your grilled cheese opens up new opportunities, since they're laden with fat and can make excellent use of leaner cheese varieties. Still, you should also consider what part of the hock to use, as some parts have more flavor than others and may require different ratios.

Typically, grilled cheese sandwiches rely on fatty, moisture-rich cheeses because they melt better than drier, aged varieties and carry that rich flavor profile. While you'll still want to use enough for a good texture, ham hocks provide plenty of decadence in their own right, so you can add a heavier sprinkle of Pecorino Romano or Parmigiano Reggiano, aged Gouda, or Manchego viejo. These underrated cheeses can cut through heavier fats more easily and are immediately noticeable even in small quantities, giving you a chance to add more complexity.

When you work with a smoked ham hock, you'll quickly notice how intense the skin's flavor is. Rich in fat and smoky flavor, this is a versatile ingredient you can mash into a spread for your bread, provided it's been properly simmered, or slice thinly and sprinkle in with shredded cheese. The meat directly under the skin is usually pinker and less potent, so it's a great choice if you're looking for more protein but not quite as much smoke. Meat from the top and bottom of the hock may offer a good middle ground, potentially holding more richness and smoke than interior meat but not quite as much as the skin, though this can vary depending on how the hock was smoked and prepared.

#9546. Drinking Tea Too Hot Could Be Bad For Your Health—Here's What To Know

Your morning cup might benefit from a little patience.

There’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health. A recently published study followed nearly half a million adults in China for almost a decade, examining how tea-drinking habits related to their health. Researchers found that regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular disease than non-tea drinkers. But one major caveat emerged: Those who reported drinking their tea “burning hot” had a higher risk of vascular disease.

According to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease. But don't give up your daily tea habit quite yet. “This study is interesting, but we don't have a proven biological explanation yet,” Dr. Niraj Patel, medical director at Clara, says.

Dr. Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.

“It doesn’t look like this study has any proposed mechanism for why burning hot tea would increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” she explains. “However, we do know that drinks that are too hot can increase the risk of esophageal cancer by creating local injury and damage.”

That concern is supported by the World Health Organization's cancer research agency, which has classified drinking beverages hotter than 149°F as probably carcinogenic to humans. The classification specifically concerns esophageal cancer, though, so it doesn't explain the connection to vascular disease identified in the new study.

The study didn’t identify a specific temperature at which drinking tea becomes detrimental to vascular health. And although researchers found an association between drinking extremely hot tea and vascular disease, that doesn't necessarily mean one causes the other.

ScienceDaily also notes that drinking tea at extremely high temperatures may diminish some of the health benefits associated with regular tea consumption.

Azarcon believes further research into tea's chemical makeup and how it may change at different temperatures could help answer some of the remaining questions.

"I'd say enjoy your tea, but don't feel like you need to drink it while it's scalding hot,” Patel suggests. “There's a difference between brewing tea with hot water and actually drinking it at that temperature. Letting it cool for a few minutes is an easy precaution and doesn't require giving up something you enjoy."

So while I don’t plan on giving up my tea habit any time soon, I am definitely making extra sure that I let my cup sit out a little longer before taking that first sip.

#9544. Upgrade Your Next Omelet With One Sweet Pantry Staple

Omelets are one of those dishes that feel made to be upgraded. While meats and vegetables go a long way toward something savory, going in a sweeter direction mixes things up and makes great use of one ingredient you probably already have on hand: honey.

A sweet omelet may sound a bit strange, but it's more common than you might think. Jelly omelets were a hit 100 years ago, and many Japanese folks love atsuyaki tamago, a rolled type of omelet that can be made with sweetened dashi stock. Using honey instead achieves a similar effect but gives you far more control over how your dish turns out. A drizzle over the top while it's still hot warms the honey, helping it spread more evenly and ensuring every bite is as sweet as you want it. Still, you can always mix a dash directly into the eggs, distributing the honey's sweetness throughout the omelet and potentially encouraging a bit of browning as it cooks.

For your first honey omelet, you may want to use something light, like honey made from orange blossom or clover nectar. These aren't overly intense and carry floral notes, and the addition of these aromas can make anyone's mouth water. If you're working with particularly rich eggs, especially duck eggs, you may want to use something with a bit more body, like wildflower or sunflower honey. These have the necessary depth of flavor to stand up to other ingredients and are great when you want a strong honey taste but not too much sweetness.

Honey can be a pretty potent ingredient, so adding too much extra sweetness with reduced tomatoes or caramelized onions can make your dish a bit too decadent in the morning. Instead, try going in the opposite direction, finding ways to add different kinds of saltiness, spice, and astringency for a complex blend of deliciousness.

A swicy flavor profile combines heat from capsaicin and sweetness from honey, both of which balance each other out and go great with eggs. Pork and honey also go together like peas and carrots, so a dollop of chorizo or spiced deli meats in an omelet brings umami, complexity, and harmonious flavors. This is a great opportunity to use hot honey as well, giving you more flexibility with other additions while still getting the same end result. Plus, spicy ingredients can add great color, improving the presentation of your dish to really wow your breakfast guests.

The best cheeses to add are usually sharp, salty, and earthy. Aged parmesan, extra-sharp cheddar, and really anything laden with salt crystals and pungency help balance the sweetness without overshadowing your honey's delicate flavors. Similarly, a bit of raw green onion can taste truly magnificent with honey and egg, but there's an emphasis on "a bit." Too much means you can't taste the honey, so try to aim for a miserly pinch at first and dial in your preference on subsequent attempts.

#9542. The 5 Healthiest Fast Food Salads, According To Nutritionists

A drive-thru doesn’t have to derail your diet.

Fast food chains aren’t exactly famous for their salads. They usually fall into two categories: a sad bowl of lettuce added to menus as an afterthought, or a vehicle for fried, calorie-dense ingredients that offset any nutritional upsides. But some chains do make an effort to sell salads worth ordering.

To identify the best better-for-you fast-food salads, we asked three nutrition experts to weigh in. Here are the menu items they recommend, along with some tips and tricks for maximizing their nutrition.

First, we need to debunk salad’s diet-friendly reputation. “A salad isn't automatically the healthiest choice on a fast food menu,” says Kathy Levin, RDN, CDCES, dipACLM, LDN. “Once you add fried chicken, bacon, cheese, candied nuts, crunchy toppings, and a creamy dressing, some salads land in the same calorie and fat range as a burger and fries.”

Taking all of those components away isn’t always a solution either. A sad salad with just lettuce and a smattering of vegetables is more like rabbit food than a satisfying meal for humans. According to Briana V. Reamer, MS, RDN, LDN, the secret is getting enough fiber, which she says “will keep you satisfied and full until your next meal.” Take advantage of the restaurant's add-ons—like beans, avocado, and more vegetables—to make your salad more substantial.

Experts also recommend watching your saturated fat intake, specifically with your protein and dressing. Grilled chicken generally has fewer calories and less saturated fat than deep-fried alternatives. Consider your dressing options, too. “If you’re not sure what to pick, look for a vinaigrette or olive-oil-based dressing,” says Tina Sergi, MS, RD, CSSD, CSCS, TSAC-F.

And, as a rule of thumb, order your dressing on the side. It keeps your salad from getting soggy on the drive home, for one, but it also gives you more portion control. “Using only part of the packet cuts saturated fat and sodium, especially when they're already on the higher end,” Sergi adds.

Of course, the dressing is only part of the equation. With those tips in mind, here are the five salads that made the cut.

This regional chain is known for its fire-grilled chicken, and this salad packs plenty of it. Each portion contains a double serving of citrus-marinated chicken breast, sliced avocado, cotija cheese, salsa fresca, and tortilla strips over a bed of greens. It's served with a creamy Mexican-inspired Caesar dressing.

El Pollo Loco strikes the right balance between substantial and light with this dish. Before you add dressing, the entire salad contains 420 calories and 52 grams of protein. “The fire-grilled chicken makes it very filling, the avocado adds heart-healthy fat and fiber, and the salsa fresca adds flavor without much sodium or sugar,” Levin says.

Like with most salads, the dressing significantly raises the calorie count—in this case, it adds 440 calories if you use the entire serving. If you're closely monitoring your daily intake, Levin advises going easy on the dressing.

Culver’s may be best known for its ButterBurgers, but experts say you shouldn’t sleep on its salads. The Chicken Cashew Salad in particular is a great choice. It starts with a bed of mixed greens, topped with cheddar, grape tomatoes, cucumbers, and roasted cashews. You can also choose from several dressings to finish it off.

With grilled chicken, the salad comes in at 430 calories and 41 grams of protein before adding dressing. Culver’s also offers six dressing varieties ranging from 50 to 260 calories.

“This is a great fiber- and protein-packed option,” says Sergi. “Plus, the cashews add healthy fats, copper to support energy production, and magnesium for optimal nerve and muscle function.”

This Lone Star staple sells a Cobb salad that’s a lighter alternative to its lineup of burgers and sandwiches. It comes loaded with all of the essentials: greens, bacon, a hard-boiled egg, grape tomatoes, carrots, and shredded cheese. You can also choose from three chicken options (the grilled chicken filet is, naturally, lighter than the fried options).

Without dressing, Whataburger's Cobb with grilled chicken has 430 calories and 44 grams of protein. It's also a source of fiber and is low in sugar, according to Reamer. “Salads high in fiber help with weight management and satisfy hunger.”

Some of Whataburger's creamier dressings add 200 to 280 calories, while the balsamic vinaigrette has 180.

For a fried chicken chain, Chick-fil-A makes some surprisingly stellar salads. The Market Salad starts with mixed greens and is topped with strawberries, blueberries, red and green apples, blue cheese, roasted almonds, and the chain’s Harvest Nut Granola. Chick-fil-A also has the most protein options on this list. The grilled chicken can come in nugget or filet form, warm or cold, and spicy or regular. Talk about variety!

The different grilled chicken options provide between 26 and 32 grams of protein, according to Chick-fil-A's nutrition guide. Levin also says you can forgo chicken entirely for a meatless meal that doesn't feel like an afterthought. “Berries and apples bring fiber, antioxidants and natural sweetness, which makes it one of the most plant-forward options on the list.”

The Market Salad is typically paired with Chick-fil-A's Zesty Apple Cider Vinaigrette Dressing, which contains 230 calories per packet. But the chain is known for its sauces, after all, so you can swap it out for another option. There's a Light Balsamic Vinaigrette with 80 calories, Fat-Free Honey Mustard with 90, and Light Italian Dressing with just 25.

Zaxby's is the third chicken chain on this list, and it stands out by offering a salad with Asian-inspired flavors. The Asian Zensation Zalad (not Salad) adds shredded carrots, cabbage, wonton strips, and Asian Slaw to mixed greens, along with a drizzle of teriyaki sauce. It also comes with a vegetable egg roll on the side.

This salad is loaded with plant-based toppings, which is why Levin also recommends the garden version as a vegetarian option. Zaxby's lists that version at 390 calories, while the grilled chicken version comes in at 530 calories and 39 grams of protein, before adding dressing.

Alongside the teriyaki drizzle, Zaxby's offers Citrus Vinaigrette with the salad, which has 110 calories per packet. It's one of the chain's lighter options. But if you're watching your calorie intake, you can swap in Lite Vinaigrette, which contains just 30 calories.

#9541. How To Build The Ultimate Aldi Charcuterie Board For Under $25

Everybody loves a charcuterie board, because a charcuterie board has a little something for everybody. But there's a certain art to building a good charcuterie board. A good board is one that offers up an array of different flavors, textures, and colors — each one complimenting the next — all coming together harmoniously to provide the ultimate grazing experience.

Charcuterie boards can add up quickly and can cost a fortune to throw together... but it's perfectly possible to create a great charcuterie board that doesn't break the bank. It all depends where you shop, and one of the best (and most affordable) places you can find your ingredients is at Aldi. In fact, you can build many a beautiful, bountiful board with just $25 thanks to Aldi's highly-rated cheeses, selection of essential cured meats, fresh fruit, crackers, and many more of Aldi's must-have products.

Need some ideas? We've got plenty of ways to build the ultimate charcuterie board that stay within this humble budget to to help make you the host with the most. Note that all of the products and prices below are sourced from an Aldi location in southern California and inventory may vary throughout the country, so be sure to double check your local store's online inventory.

If you want to stick to the tried and true, classic charcuterie board ingredients, you can gather all the hits at Aldi for $25 and build a beautiful board. First (and arguable the most important) stop is the cheese. With Aldi's affordable prices, you can feature three different cheeses which will give the board enough variety — ideally, a classic board combines both soft and hard cheese.

Aldi's private-label brand Emporium Selection has three different cheeses that will not only go together lovely, but will satisfy different tastes and preferences: The Garlic & Herb Gourmet Spreadable Cheese, the Smoked Gouda Cheese, and the Aged Reserved White Cheddar Cheese (it's America's favorite cheese, after all).

When it comes to the meat, you can't go wrong with a Salami Trio; you'll get the most bang for your buck here by being able to offer three different types of salami on your board (Black Peppercorn, Smoked Calabrese, and Double Smoked Salami). And now that you have the main events, it's just a matter of filling the board in with two more essential items. Grapes will add some freshness and sweetness, complimenting the salty meat and cheese, Aldi's Rosemary Flatbread Crackers will be the perfect accompaniment for everything else.

If you're looking to serve up something more seasonal, Aldi is full of great fall finds that will work splendidly on a charcuterie board. And thanks to the extremely reasonable prices, you can actually cram a lot of different items onto this board so that it's overflowing with fall flavors.

Starting with your cheeses, three seasonal picks will be the centerpieces: a Cheddar Parmesan Cheese ($3.95) that will go with all of your other flavors, a 1,000 Day Aged Gouda ($3.99) for that sharp bite, and a Crimson Cranberry White Stilton ($4.19) to really bring it home. For the meat, Aldi's Honey & Bourbon Cocktail Salami ($3.29) is the perfect choice to bring in some of those comforting fall notes.

Candied Pecans ($4.39) and Fig Fruit Spread ($3.29) will add some sweetness to the board, and you can brighten things up a bit with a few fresh seasonal Bartlett Pears ($3.29). Grab some of Aldi's Sea Salt Scalloped Crackers ($1.99) that'll work perfectly with any combo, and you've got yourself one great fall-flavored charcuterie board.

Are you cooking up an Italian dinner, or just in the mood for some salty, briny antipasti appetizers? You can create a charcuterie board version of Italian antipasti with several Italian-inspired favorites that you can find at Aldi, and snack like you're in Italy while keeping it all under $25.

For your cheese selection, a fresh log of mozzarella cheese ($3.25) will be the perfect counterpart to the nutty, salty authentic Parmigiano-Reggiano ($6.05) (which is different from Parmesan). And with several types of Italian-imported cured meats available, you can offer up some options like Priano's Prosciutto Italiano ($3.55) and Speck Italiano ($3.55).

Outside of the meat and cheese, Aldi actually has a ready-made medley of antipasti olives ($2.85) which includes black and green pitted olives, provolone cheese cubes, button mushrooms, and roasted red peppers — giving your board lots of variety and bang for your buck. Aldi's Artichoke Bruschetta ($3.09) is the perfect dip-able, spreadable item to accompany everything, along with some Sea Salt & Olive Oil Italian Breadsticks ($2.19) for crispy, crunchy bites.

If you're feeling a little French, bring some French countryside charm to a rustic charcuterie board using an array of Aldi products that will give your guests a little taste of France. Because who doesn't want that?

You can go for the French trifecta of cheeses for this one: a double creme brie ($4.39), a buttery camembert ($4.39), and a smoked Gruyere ($4.39). This will give your board a mix of soft and hard cheeses, each with its own unique flavor to keep the tastebuds on their toes. Stick to a classic salami to compliment the bolder flavors of the cheese, and if you want to level things up you can always bake the brie (which you can even do in your microwave).

Then include some classic French ingredients for those added touches that'll transport you to France. Aldi's Herb Cornichons ($3.29) and Burman's Sweet Honey Dijon Mustard ($1.75) will taste delicious served alongside your meat and cheese, and then you can freshen things up a bit with red grapes ($1.69 / pound). Now all you need is the perfect vehicle to carry all of these French goodies: Aldi's Original Brioche Style Mini Toasts ($1.89).

One last stop in the Mediterranean. You can combine all of the delicious Mediterranean-inspired items at Aldi to build a board that transforms charcuterie into a delectable mezze spread.

When it comes to the cheese, there's one clear star here: feta. You can represent it two ways in one board by grabbing the Tomato and Basil Feta Cheese Block ($3.95) and the Greek Feta Salad ($2.59) (made with Kalamata and green olives and cubes of feta marinated in herbs and spices). And the Dry Aged Fennel Mediterranean Style Salami ($3.99) is the no-brainer choice for this board's protein.

From there, focus on the delicious dips that make mezze what it is. Go for Aldi's Olive Tapenade Hummus ($2.85) to double down on those salty olives, and brighten up the board with a Cucumber Dill Tzatziki Dip ($3.29) made with Greek yogurt. Throw in some Deli-Sliced Roasted Red Peppers ($3.19) as an accompaniment, and don't forget everyone's favorite part: The pita bread ($2.85)! Pro tip: Throw 'em in the oven for a few minutes and serve them warm; it makes all the difference.

Make the holidays even more festive with a holiday-themed charcuterie board that'll look (and taste) the part. Whether you're looking to serve something beautiful at your holiday party or you want to dive into those festive flavors while you can, Aldi has tons of options to choose from that scream holiday season.

Start with Aldi's Cranberry Cinnamon Flavored Goat Cheese Log ($3.85) (because what says holiday more than that combo?), and balance it out with the Cabot Seriously Sharp Cheddar Cheese for that sharpness everyone wants on a charcuterie board, plus some extra creaminess in the Double Crème Brie Cheese ($4.39). For the cured meat, you can stick with a classic prosciutto ($3.59), and accompany the main events with some warm and cozy flavors like Aldi's Caramelized Red Onion Chutney ($2.99) for sweetness and Honey Roasted Nut Blend ($5.29) for extra crunch.

And, last but not least, choose a tasty whole pomegranate ($1.89) to give your board a pop of sweetness as well as a pop of color — leave one half in tact and place it on your board cut-side open; it'll look beautiful. Here's how to pick the best pomegranate for your board.

Okay, so this may not technically qualify as a charcuterie board, but that term tends to be very forgiving these days. For all those veggie lovers out there, you can build a meatless, vegetable-forward board at Aldi that'll give everyone a fresh taste of the garden and still keep things interesting.

Aldi's Roasted Garlic & Tomato Basil Monterey Jack Cheese ($3.49) and Onion & Chive Double Gloucester Cheese ($4.19) are a great duo to anchor this board, and a Spinach Artichoke Dip ($2.99) adds even more flavor and creaminess. Along with Aldi's Garden Vegetable Crackers ($1.79), you can serve up all of your herby, cheesy goodness with some fresh crudités using Gourmet Mixed Baby Carrots ($2.99) (which happen to be adorable) and a pound of radishes ($1.45) for added crisp and color. For that last flavorful munch, throw in the Garlic & Herb Nut Blend ($5.29), which includes seasoned pecans, almonds, and cashews.

Charcuterie can be a morning thing too! When it comes to brunch, pretty much anything goes... so why not turn the meal into a flavorful board of breakfast delights? This one gets a little creative and combines sweet, salty, herby, and smoky for the perfect brunch munching.

Instead of your typical bread or crackers, you can build this board around Aldi's mini bagels ($3.85), which will be the perfect vehicle for soft, herby cheeses like everybody's favorite Boursin Garlic & Fine Herb Cheese ($6.05) and a Chive & Onion Cream Cheese Spread ($1.99). To round it all out, opt for the jam or preserves of your choice (we like blueberry preserves, $3.09) and incorporate some fresh blackberries ($1.69) to give everyone their morning serving of fruit.

Some like it hot, and those people can find plenty of options at Aldi to set their mouths on fire. Make things (painfully) fun with a spiced-up charcuterie board featuring some of Aldi's hot and spicy products.

Begin the spice-loving journey with Aldi's 3 Chili Gouda Cheese ($3.85) paired with the Tequila & Ghost Pepper Cocktail Salami ($3.29): A killer combo. Next, grab the Stuffed Green Pepperoncini ($3.99) — these will be a great addition because they're a little briny and spicy, but they're made with Herbes de Provence and filled with cream cheese, which will offer a bit of a respite from the heat.

Now for the dips, include the Hot Honey Dip ($2.79) for a bit of sweet heat, and the Piquillo Pepper & Artichoke Bruschetta ($3.09) for another delicious element that offers a bit more sweetness than spice to balance things out. Finish it all off with Aldi's Sea Salt & Pepper Scalloped Crackers ($1.99) for dipping and dunking.

Pickled and pickle-flavored foods seem to be all the rage lately, so why not lean in? Turn your party into a pickle party by building a fully pickled-out charcuterie board at Aldi for that punchy hit of briny, vinegary goodness.

From there, you obviously need some actual pickles. Go for Great Gherkins Kosher Baby Whole Dill Pickles ($2.09), which are the perfect size for snacking. Stick to Aldi's Original Crisp Crackers ($1.79) to accompany everything so your cracker doesn't compete with all of the flavors you've already got going on.

Lastly, for all those out there with a sweet tooth, there are lots of ways to incorporate notes of sweetness into your "charcuterie" board while still keeping it fairly savory (this one foregoes the meat as well). If you love sweet but don't want to go full dessert board, this board is for you.

#9538. 5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

Let's just say the health department had a few notes.

Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety issues.

I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety issues. The company paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

Records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow company food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

In February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such issues can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

In 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the issues found overseas!)

Sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

More recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

Big Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety issues over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

The Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

Wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

Perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

Even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

A bowl of chili welcomes a wide array of renditions. You can make the dish red or green, use proteins like turkey, pork, or chicken instead of the classic beef, and include many aromatics in the mix. Each detail makes a chili rendition unique. Even a fresh herb gives a bowl a whole new character — just look toward Ina Garten's inclusion of basil. Ina Garten often uses basil as a swap for cilantro, so her inclusion of the herb in her chili makes sense.

Using the Mediterranean herb in the Tex-Mex recipe may sound unusual, but the flavors align surprisingly well. Garten uses basil's mildly citrusy sweet and lightly peppery flavor specifically in a chicken-based chili, integrating the herb during both the initial simmering stage and as a final garnish. It's a one-two combo that establishes an herbal character that infuses into every bite, lending more than just a basil-inflected finish.

Garten's rendition works the basil into a tomato sauce base, full of sweet bell peppers and onions, lightly recalling a pasta sauce in composition. Still, seasonings like cumin, chili powder, and a dash of spicy cayenne appear in the mix, cementing the dish as a bowl of chili, only brighter and more herbal in nature.

Ina Garten's tips for cooking chicken perfectly dependably deliver, but don't rule out employing the basil in chili recipes with other proteins, too. The herb also works well in an extra-hearty bean and brisket rendition that's spiced with chiles and even coffee. Cooked down right alongside the kidney beans, basil lends the legumes its distinct herbal character, all without becoming a cornerstone flavor. You can try out such a technique in a classic ground beef chili, too; using the herb early in cooking makes it one of many layered flavors.

If you're after a more basil-forward spin, consider working the herb into a ground turkey chili recipe. You can still go heavy on the spice, using chili powder and jalapeños alongside garlic powder and cumin. Add dried basil early on and raw basil atop the finished chili, and you'll get a delicate bowl, herbal-tasting and fresh, yet still pretty classic.

And for a more inventive approach, take a page from Thai cuisine, specifically Phat ka-phrao (stir-fried basil beef). Made with sturdier Thai basil, this version of the herb stands up better to heat. Saute the meat alongside extra-spicy chiles, lots of garlic, and this type of basil, and you can lay down the foundation for an extra-bold chili, still delicious over rice or with tortilla chips.

#9533. Upgrade Tuna Salad With A Boxed Ingredient That Improves Texture

Tuna salad is a pragmatic yet delicious dish, easily crafted using pantry staples. Open up some canned fish packed in oil or water, mix with store-bought mayo, then fold in some aromatics, and you'll have yourself a tasty classic. It's a tried-and-true formula that welcomes many other shelf-stable components, like panko bread crumbs, for example. You only need about 2 tablespoons per can of tuna to round things out nicely.

The delicate breadcrumb style is wonderfully versatile in the kitchen, and its texture enhances tuna salad, too. The foodstuff lends the dish more body, without turning it too dense. The panko absorbs moisture, making the crumbs turn soft while still retaining airiness, in turn creating an extra-tender salad. The panko also thickens the dish, giving your meal more structure. Not to mention, a bite here or there might still remain crunchy, upping the textural intrigue.

It's an advantageous set of qualities unique specifically to panko; you won't want to reach for a different breadcrumb in this application, as they may be too dense. This Japanese foodstuff is made using a unique electric cooking process, producing a delicate crumble without any bread crust. Other breadcrumb varieties are simply too heavy for the task. So grab a package of panko online or in stores to make a tuna salad rendition with a textural twist.

Not sure how to round out a tuna salad with panko? The options are wide-ranging. You could keep to a straightforward mix of tuna, mayo, salt, and pepper — perfect for a tuna sandwich filling — or go with the many potential tuna salad upgrades. Walnuts or kimchi, for example, add body and even more texture to the dish.

Similarly, to complement panko's delicate composition, throw in some vegetables. Green onion, celery, and an herb, say parsley, dill, or cilantro, are tried-and-true tuna salad enhancements. And don't overlook a tangy fermented bite, whether in the form of pickles or pickled onions for a truly amped up tuna salad. You could also imbue brightness using vinegar or even lime juice, which will aromatically soak into the panko.

Alternatively, consider playing to the breadcrumb's East Asian origins, using other Japanese ingredients in the dish. You could add a couple spoonfuls of miso into the dressing for complex savory flavors, as well as sesame seeds and oil for a discernible nutty touch. Or go down the spicy tuna route, incorporating a hot sauce like Sriracha into the build — especially tasty when wrapped in seaweed. Swap the standard mayo for a Japanese-style emulsion, mix in the panko, and you'll have yourself a magical tuna salad foundation.

#9531. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9530. Scrambled Eggs Get A Major Protein And Flavor Boost When You Add This Omega-Rich Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When many of us think "hot breakfast," we tend to naturally gravitate toward thoughts of scrambled eggs. Aside from the fact that, when prepared correctly, they are tender, delicate, and fluffy (or custardy, depending on how you like them), eggs are considered the gold standard for protein, so they are quite wholesome as well. On their own, though, they can get a little monotonous, especially if you're making them every day, so it does help to add an ingredient here or there. And if you happen to enjoy omega-3-rich cold-smoked salmon, well, it pairs seamlessly with a classic scramble, boosting both the flavor and the protein content.

Once considered an expensive delicacy, smoked salmon is quite popular now in the U.S., and as a result, it's much easier to find at your local grocery store (even Aldi carries its own version, and it can be found at Walmart, too). Cold-smoked salmon, despite the fact that it tends to be packed in super-thin slices, is buttery and velvety. While it does taste fishy, there are also light, smoky notes that give it a deeply savory flavor, which works beautifully when combined with the mild egg scramble. Additionally, a serving (which will vary in size) might contain anywhere from 12 to 18 grams of protein, which is great if you have daily goals you want to meet or you're just looking to get more of the macronutrient in general.

Truly, the most difficult part about incorporating smoked salmon into your scramble is cooking the eggs to the right consistency without burning or browning them. All you have to do with the salmon is slice the ultra-thin pieces into slivers or small squares. Once your eggs have reached the texture you desire, you'll take the pan off the heat and fold in the salmon. That's literally it; you don't have to actually cook the salmon over direct heat because it's so delicate that the residual warmth of the scrambled eggs will gently bring it up to temperature.

Now, because smoked salmon is so light and thin, you might want your eggs to match that energy, so create a fluffy, soft texture with a bit of cream whisked in. Alternatively, you could take a page out of Bobby Flay's book and fold in a dollop of crème fraîche, or really up the decadence and melt in some cubes of cream cheese (and take care not to overcook anything, because smoked salmon with burnt, rubbery eggs? No thanks). Also, because all of the elements involved are either rich or thick, a sprinkling of something green, like fresh chives or dill, or even a little parsley or tarragon, would brighten things up, both aesthetically and in terms of flavor.

#9528. Papa Johns Wants Your Honest Opinion—And It's Offering Free Pizza In Return

They're asking for the good, the bad, and everything in between.

Opening a pizza box can bring out the critic in anyone. But whatever your reaction, whether it's about a pale crust or toppings piled onto one side, Papa Johns wants to hear about it—and your opinion could be worth a whole other pizza.

The chain has launched a two-week promotion called "Snap a Pizza, Get a Free Pizza," inviting customers to snap a photo of their orders and tell the company what they really think. You can praise it, complain about it, or land somewhere in the middle. Even a less-than-glowing review is welcome.

Before you start snapping pictures of every slice in sight, though, there's some fine print worth reading.

To participate, you'll need to spend at least $15 on an order placed through the Papa Johns website or app. You'll also need a Papa Rewards account with text messages enabled, since that's how the chain will contact you about submitting your review.

Papa Johns wants an unedited photo of your pizza, along with your thoughts on everything from the level of cheese and how it's cooked to the overall experience. Once the photo is approved, you'll receive an offer for a large one-topping pizza in your Rewards account.

That word "free" does come with a qualification. Redeeming your reward requires spending at least $5 on your next order, meaning you'll have to open your wallet twice. Still, if you've ever had strong opinions about the way your pizza arrived, you might as well get something out of sharing them.

Of course, Papa Johns is getting something out of this arrangement, too. All those pictures and reviews give the chain a closer look at what customers are actually receiving.

"We see the pizza pics, the unboxings and the hot takes online every day, and we know our customers aren't shy about sharing what they think," said Chris Lyn-Sue, Papa Johns' global chief marketing officer, in a statement.The promotion is part of Papa Johns' recently announced "Unbox Better" initiative, which focuses on things like food quality and the chain’s general service. It's also not the only fast food chain inviting customers to speak their minds. Earlier this year, Burger King went so far as to encourage customers to call or text its president directly with their feedback.

Papa Johns is offering a slightly different incentive, although I suspect a free pizza might convince a few more people to participate.

#9527. Forget Expensive Ribeye: A Cheaper Cut For Delicious Beef Stroganoff

Indulgently and immensely comforting, beef stroganoff is one of those low-effort meals you make when you just want to feel good. But one thing that might not lift your spirits is the price. Classic stroganoff starts off with strips of thinly sliced beef, with cuts like ribeye being among the best picks. We're not here to fault ribeye, which has earned its price for a reason, but if you want to knock a few dollars off your next batch, try swapping in ground beef instead.

While it may not satisfy the purist, and might even horrify a Russian (the dish's country of origin), we'd argue that ground beef is a worthy alternative to any traditional whole cut of steak. The texture is bound to be different, and you'll need to adjust how you cook it, but good-quality ground beef still has the rich, beefy flavor that pairs so well with the tang of sour cream, earthy mushrooms, and the sweet depth of cooked-down onions, all at a significantly lower cost.

Another reason ground beef works so well here is its cooking time. Traditional beef stroganoff relies on expensive cuts that are prized for their tenderness and quick-cooking nature. Cheaper, tougher cuts like chuck or round usually need hours of braising to soften, which doesn't suit a dish that's meant to come together quickly. Ground beef, however, is often made from those same economical cuts, and the grinding process does all the tenderizing mechanically. That means you're getting all that mouthwatering flavor without the waiting, guaranteeing a tasty, Boomer-approved meal.

If you make the switch from ribeye to ground beef, you'll want to do a few things differently. First, check out the numbers on your ground beef packaging. You're looking for a blend that doesn't shy away from fat, something like an 80-to-20 lean-to-fat ratio, or even 70-to-30. Like ribeye, these fattier blends are packed with rich flavor, and the fat that'll render out will elevate the sauce, just in a different format. Go any leaner and you risk dry, chewy beef pebbles floating in your sauce.

With ribeye, standard practice is to slice the beef ultra-thin, give it a quick sear, then let it simmer in the sauce for a few minutes. The process for ground beef is similar, albeit with a few caveats. For starters, there's no slicing, so you're already saving time. Like ribeye, you want to get the meat nicely browned. Our personal advice is to add the beef to the pan in small handfuls and flatten each one with the back of a spoon, which allows it to brown without overcrowding the pan.

Remove the beef from the pan once it's seared, which isn't usually done with ribeye. Even in a fattier blend, ground beef has far more exposed surface area than your average slice of steak, so it risks drying out if it's left to simmer for too long. For the most tender results, build your sauce first, then add the beef back in and stir once you're just about ready to serve. Don't worry about the flavors not melding, since the fat and fond left behind from searing will be doing most of the heavy lifting.

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($25,500 in 2027), HSA ($4,500 individual / $9,000 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $25,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

Most employers allow you to change your 401(k) contribution rate at any time. Increasing by 2% of salary is small enough that you will barely notice the paycheck reduction, but it compounds dramatically over time. Repeat this increase every six months until you are maxing out your 401(k).

Roughly one in four employees leaves free employer match money on the table. If your employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary, you need to contribute at least 6% to capture the full match. This is an instant 50% return on your money — no investment can beat it.

A Roth IRA provides tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, with no required minimum distributions. The 2026 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+). If your income exceeds the Roth limits, use the backdoor Roth conversion strategy to contribute indirectly.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The national median for under-35 is only $13,000, so if you have more than that, you are already ahead of most peers.

The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

Generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

It is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $75,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

#9524. This Chain Serves The Best Old-School Italian Sub, According To Customer Reviews

You might not expect it, but sandwich chains are holding it down when it comes to Italian subs. Of course, there is no denying the appeal of a small, locally owned shop, but there are many reasons why you might opt instead to head into a chain to get your Italian hoagie fix, the most obvious of which is proximity. But there is also the fact that some chains just make darn good food. Food Republic did its research and compiled a list of the best chain Italian subs based on customer reviews, and each entry brings its own unique flavor to the table. But only one, the No. 13 Original Italian from Jersey Mike's, can claim to be the best old-school version of this particular sub.

"They do it right," one Reddit user said, referencing the Original Italian. They continued by stating that if they had a classic Italian deli near them, they'd go there, but since they don't, "it's Jersey Mike's without question." Another user in that same thread agreed, writing, "I love this sub and am always a little amazed [it comes from] a chain" and not, presumably, from a traditional deli. And over on Google, a reviewer shared that the Original Italian reminded them of a sub they'd had during their childhood and expressed their gratitude that "there is a place that can make a real Italian hero like the old days."

It's worth noting that an old-school-style Italian sub owes it all to the Italian immigrants who populated this country throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. There are a few stories about how the hoagie came to be, including one based in Philadelphia (where it's the official sandwich of the city) involving shipyard workers and their distinctive lunches. There is another version that describes how Giovanna Amato sold filling sandwiches to dockworkers in Maine. Whatever its origins, the classic Italian sub came to be characterized by Italian meats and cheeses, a variety of fresh, crisp vegetables, a savory dressing, and an oily, vinegary drizzle.

Jersey Mike's Original Italian proves a chain can still honor those old-school roots. It checks every box, from five different Italian meats to provolone cheese to the default setting, Mike's Way, which includes onions, lettuce sliced super-thin, and tomatoes, as well as red wine vinegar and an olive oil blend, plus two impactful seasonings: salt and oregano.

But of course, Jersey Mike's serves 21st-century customers who like having options, so the sandwich, in addition to scratching an old-school itch, can also serve as a jumping-off point for some. You might, for example, upgrade your Original Italian sub by choosing the rosemary parmesan bread instead of plain white. There are a number of additional toppings available as well, such as jalapeño peppers, dill pickles, and hot chopped pepper relish.
